lessons.title: Understanding the Egg Laying Cycle
lessons.body: A hen's egg laying cycle is a daily rhythm that starts when she reaches sexual maturity, usually around 18 to 22 weeks of age, depending on breed and management. In Africa, many smallholder farmers use indigenous or improved breeds like Isa Brown, Lohmann Brown, or Kuroiler. The cycle begins with the hen ovulating a yolk into the oviduct. Over the next 24 to 26 hours, the egg white (albumen), shell membranes, and shell are added. The egg is then laid, and the process repeats. Most hens lay in the morning, with peak production between 7 am and 11 am. A healthy hen can lay 5 to 6 eggs per week during her peak, but this drops with age. The first year of lay is the most productive; after 12 months, production declines by about 10-15% per year. To manage this, farmers often keep hens for one or two laying cycles, then cull or molt. In Africa, where feed costs are high, many farmers use forced molting to extend lay, but this requires careful nutrition and lighting. Understanding the cycle helps you time feed, lighting, and nest box management. For example, provide 16 hours of light daily during peak lay to stimulate ovulation. Keep stress low: sudden noise, predators, or moving hens can delay or stop laying for days. Track your flock's lay percentage: if you have 100 hens, expect 80-90 eggs per day at peak. If it drops below 60, investigate immediately. Record daily egg counts to spot trends early.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Egg Production and Persistency
lessons.body: Egg production and persistencyâhow long a hen keeps laying wellâdepend on several factors you can control. First, nutrition: a laying hen needs 16-18% protein, 3.5-4.5% calcium, and 0.4-0.5% available phosphorus. In Africa, many farmers mix their own feed using maize, soybean meal, fishmeal, and limestone. A common mistake is insufficient calcium, leading to thin shells and fewer eggs. Provide oyster shell or limestone grit free-choice. Second, lighting: hens need 14-16 hours of light daily to maintain lay. If you rely on natural daylight, expect lower production in winter or rainy seasons. Use a bulb (e.g., 40-watt LED) per 20 square meters to extend light. Third, temperature: heat stress above 30Â°C reduces feed intake and egg numbers. Provide shade, ventilation, and cool water. Fourth, water: a hen drinks up to 250 ml daily; lack of clean water for even a few hours can drop production. Fifth, disease: Newcastle, infectious bronchitis, and worms reduce lay. Vaccinate and deworm regularly. Sixth, age: persistency is highest in the first 20 weeks of lay, then declines. Replace hens after 80 weeks. Seventh, stress: moving, overcrowding, or predators cause drops. Keep 4-5 hens per square meter in deep litter. Finally, breed: hybrid layers like Isa Brown outlay indigenous breeds. With good management, you can achieve 85% lay persistency for 12 months. Record daily egg numbers and feed intake to spot problems early.

lessons.title: Egg Collection, Handling, and Storage
lessons.body: Collect eggs at least twice dailyâmorning and afternoonâto prevent breakage, dirt, and heat damage. In Africa, where temperatures often exceed 30Â°C, eggs left in nests for hours lose quality fast. Use clean, dry hands or a soft basket. Never stack eggs more than 5 high. After collection, sort out cracked, dirty, or abnormal eggs. Do not wash eggs unless necessary; washing removes the protective bloom and invites bacteria. If eggs are dirty, wipe with a dry cloth or use fine sandpaper. For storage, keep eggs at 15-18Â°C and 70-80% humidity. In rural areas without refrigerators, store in a cool, dark room, e.g., a ventilated mud-brick store or a clay pot with a lid. You can also use evaporative cooling: place eggs in a porous pot surrounded by wet sand. Never store eggs near onions, kerosene, or chemicalsâthey absorb odours. For sale, keep eggs in clean trays or cartons. If you sell at local markets, transport in padded crates to avoid cracks. For longer storage, use refrigeration at 4-7Â°C, but only if eggs are clean and dry. Remember: eggs stored at room temperature lose quality faster; after 7 days, the air cell grows and albumen thins. For best quality, sell within 3 days. If you keep eggs for hatching, store at 15-18Â°C and turn daily for up to 7 days. Always label collection dates. Good handling reduces losses by up to 20% and earns better prices.

lessons.title: Egg Grading, Sizing, and Packaging
lessons.body: Grading eggs by size and quality helps you get better prices. In Africa, markets often pay more for large, clean, uncracked eggs. Grade by weight: small (under 53g), medium (53-63g), large (63-73g), and extra-large (over 73g). Use a simple egg scale or a kitchen scale. For quality, check shell cleanliness, shape, and texture. Reject eggs with cracks, rough shells, or abnormal shapes. Also check internal quality by candling: in a dark room, hold the egg against a bright light (torch or candle). A fresh egg has a small air cell (less than 5mm) and a clear, firm yolk. If the air cell is large or the yolk moves freely, the egg is old. For packaging, use clean, dry trays or cartons. In many African countries, 30-egg trays are standard. Label with grade, date, and your farm name. For retail, consider 6- or 12-egg cartons. Packaging protects eggs during transport and shows professionalism. If you sell to hotels or supermarkets, they may require specific grading and packaging. Invest in a simple egg candler and scaleâthey cost little and improve your marketability. Also, train workers to handle eggs gently. Remember: graded eggs sell faster and at higher prices. Even in local markets, customers prefer uniform, clean eggs. So sort, grade, and package neatly.

lessons.title: Quality Control: Shell Integrity and Internal Quality
lessons.body: Quality control starts with the shell. A strong shell protects the egg from bacteria and breakage. Shell strength depends on calcium, phosphorus, and vitamin D3 in the diet. Provide limestone or oyster shell free-choice, and ensure hens get sunlight or vitamin D3 supplement. Avoid stressing hensâstress reduces shell quality. Collect eggs gently and check for cracks by tapping two eggs together; a dull sound means a crack. Discard cracked eggs for sale; use them immediately in your home or sell for processing. For internal quality, candling is key. A fresh egg has a small air cell, a firm yolk that stays centered, and thick albumen. As eggs age, the air cell grows, the yolk flattens, and albumen thins. To check freshness without candling, place the egg in a bowl of water: fresh eggs sink, old eggs float. For selling, aim for eggs less than 7 days old. Store at cool temperatures and high humidity. Also, keep nest boxes clean and change bedding regularly to prevent dirty eggs. Dirty eggs carry bacteria like Salmonella. If you must clean, use a dry method or sanitize with a warm, mild bleach solution (1 teaspoon per liter) and dry immediately. Never soak eggs. For internal quality, avoid feeding hens excessive cottonseed meal or other toxins that cause off-flavours. Regularly test a few eggs by breaking them open: look for blood spots, meat spots, or abnormal colours. These are usually harmless but reduce consumer acceptance. Maintain records of quality checks and train workers. Good quality control reduces waste and builds customer trust.

lessons.title: Dealing with Abnormal Eggs and Production Drops
lessons.body: Abnormal eggs and sudden drops in production are common challenges. Abnormal eggs include: soft-shelled, shell-less, double-yolked, small, misshapen, or eggs with rough shells. Soft-shelled eggs often result from calcium deficiency, stress, or disease like infectious bronchitis. Double-yolked eggs occur when two yolks are released too close together; they are safe to eat but not for hatching. Small eggs may come from young hens or stress. To fix, adjust diet: add limestone grit, ensure 4% calcium in feed, and provide vitamin D3. Also, reduce stress by keeping consistent lighting and avoiding sudden changes. Production drops can be caused by many factors: disease (Newcastle, avian influenza, worms), poor nutrition, heat stress, lack of water, predators, or aging. If your flock's lay drops by more than 10% in a week, act fast. Check water and feed quality, look for signs of disease (e.g., green droppings, coughing), and review lighting. Deworm if needed. In Africa, heat stress is a major cause; provide shade, increase ventilation, and offer cool water. Also, check for external parasites like mites and liceâthey suck blood and reduce lay. Treat with appropriate acaricides. If hens are older than 80 weeks, consider culling or forced molting. Keep daily records of egg numbers, feed intake, and mortality. This helps you pinpoint the cause. For abnormal eggs, collect and dispose of them properly; do not sell cracked or soft-shelled eggs. If you see many abnormal eggs, consult a vet or extension officer. Early action saves your flock and income.

quiz.q: At what age do layer hens typically start laying eggs?
quiz.explanation: Most layer breeds reach sexual maturity and begin laying between 18 and 22 weeks of age.

quiz.q: How many hours of light per day do laying hens need for optimal production?
quiz.explanation: Laying hens require 14-16 hours of light daily to stimulate and maintain egg production.

quiz.q: What is the recommended calcium level in layer feed?
quiz.explanation: Layer feed should contain 3.5-4.5% calcium to support strong shell formation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of heat stress in layers?
quiz.explanation: Heat stress reduces feed intake and egg production in laying hens.

quiz.q: How often should you collect eggs in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: Collecting eggs at least twice daily prevents heat damage and breakage in hot climates.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid washing eggs?
options: B) It removes the protective bloom
C) It changes the shell colour
quiz.explanation: Washing removes the natural bloom that protects eggs from bacteria.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for eggs without refrigeration?
quiz.explanation: Eggs store best at 15-18Â°C in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place.

quiz.q: What does a small air cell in a candled egg indicate?
quiz.explanation: A small air cell (less than 5mm) indicates a fresh egg.

quiz.q: What is the standard weight range for a large egg?
quiz.explanation: Large eggs typically weigh between 63 and 73 grams.

quiz.q: Which method is used to check internal egg quality?
quiz.explanation: Candling involves shining a light through the egg to inspect the air cell and yolk.

quiz.q: What causes soft-shelled eggs?
quiz.explanation: Soft-shelled eggs are often caused by a lack of calcium in the diet.

quiz.q: What should you do if your flock's egg production drops by more than 10% in a week?
quiz.explanation: A sudden drop indicates a problem; check water, feed, disease, and stress factors.

quiz.q: Which disease commonly causes a drop in egg production?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle disease is a viral infection that severely reduces egg production.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of double-yolked eggs?
options: A) Two yolks released too close together
quiz.explanation: Double-yolked eggs occur when two yolks are released in quick succession.

quiz.q: How can you prevent dirty eggs?
quiz.explanation: Clean nest boxes with fresh bedding reduce dirt on eggs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended space per hen in deep litter?
quiz.explanation: Provide 4-5 hens per square meter to reduce stress and overcrowding.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is essential for strong eggshells?
quiz.explanation: Calcium is the primary mineral for shell formation.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store eggs in rural areas without electricity?
options: B) In a cool, dark room
quiz.explanation: A cool, dark, ventilated room helps maintain egg quality.

quiz.q: What does a floating egg in water indicate?
quiz.explanation: Old eggs have larger air cells and float in water.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an abnormal egg?
quiz.explanation: Soft-shelled eggs are abnormal and indicate a problem.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm layers?
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming every 2-3 months prevents internal parasites that reduce lay.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity for egg storage?
quiz.explanation: 70-80% relative humidity helps prevent egg dehydration.

quiz.q: Which factor can cause a sudden drop in egg production?
quiz.explanation: Predator attacks stress hens and can cause a sharp drop in laying.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of candling eggs?
quiz.explanation: Candling uses light to inspect the air cell, yolk, and albumen for quality.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a fresh egg?
quiz.explanation: Fresh eggs have a firm, centered yolk and thick albumen.

quiz.q: What should you do with cracked eggs?
options: A) Sell them at full price
B) Use them immediately or discard
C) Store them for a week
quiz.explanation: Cracked eggs are prone to bacteria; use immediately or discard.

quiz.q: How can you reduce heat stress in layers?
quiz.explanation: Shade and good ventilation help hens cope with high temperatures.

quiz.q: What is the typical peak lay percentage for a good flock?
quiz.explanation: A well-managed flock can achieve 80-90% lay at peak production.

quiz.q: Which external parasite affects egg production?
quiz.explanation: Mites and lice suck blood, causing stress and reduced laying.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage time for eggs at room temperature?
quiz.explanation: Eggs stored at room temperature maintain quality for about 7 days.
